What's moving the market: Singapore's biggest property deals and hottest searches (Oct 2)
article:
Here is this week’s data-led look at Singapore’s property market, covering record transactions, rental benchmarks and the most searched homes on EdgeProp.

The following insights are compiled from EdgeProp Buddy , URA Realis and data.gov.sg, downloaded as of Sept 30.

Non-landed private homes — new launches, resales and rents

The highest priced condo unit transacted in the past 14 days was a 29th-floor apartment at Sculptura Ardmore , fetching $20 million. That works out to about $6,112 psf on its floor area of 3,272 sq ft.

It is also among the highest psf prices achieved at the freehold condo. Last year, two units were likewise resold for $20 million each, translating to $6,193 psf for the 31st-floor unit in November and $6,013 psf for the 26th-floor unit in June 2025.

Situated in the Ardmore Park enclave in District 10, Sculptura Ardmore consists of 34 units and was completed in 2014.

Next among the most expensive condo units transacted was a unit at Grange Residences fetching $9.25 million, followed by an apartment at The Draycott which went for $6.36 million. Both are also situated within District 10.

Among condos in the Rest of Central region (RCR) or city fringe, Stirling Residences was the most popular with tenants, with 77 rental deals inked. This was followed by Normanton Park , Commonwealth Towers and Park Colonial with 66, 51 and 51 contracts respectively starting August 2026.

Condo units with the highest rents in RCR, based on latest available data for August 2026 contracts, included an apartment at Corals At Keppel Bay which commanded $24,800 per month.

Also in the Keppel Bay waterfront precinct, two units at Reflections At Keppel Bay made the list, bringing in $22,500 and $19,600 in monthly rent. An apartment at Caribbean At Keppel Bay was leased out for $16,500.

Meanwhile, a 5,450 sq ft, five-bedroom unit at The Meyerise in District 15 fetched $23,000 in monthly rent, or $4.22 psf on its floor area.

Landed homes — highest transacted prices and rents

Within the Singapore landed property market, the highest-priced transaction in the past 14 days to Sept 30 was for a house on Oriole Crescent near the Bukit Timah education belt. The landed home was sold for $24 million, or $2,155 psf.

A stone’s throw away, Vanda Drive produced the fortnight’s second-most expensive landed property deal, with a house on the street fetching nearly $13.69 million or $2,817 psf.

Located off Dunearn Road, both houses are near schools such as Nanyang Girls’ High School, Hwa Chong Institution and Raffles Girls’ Primary School.

Over on Luxus Hills Heights, three new sales involving terrace houses also made the list of priciest landed deals during the period in review. They were sold on Sept 19 for $6.585 million, $6.725 million and $7.072 million.

They are part of Luxus Hills, a 999-year leasehold landed housing estate situated off Ang Mo Kio Avenue 5. The developer recently launched the latest phase, Phase 10, after the private preview began in end-July.

HDB flats — top prices and rents, most transacted blocks

The highest-priced HDB resale flats over the past two weeks included a five-room flat at Block 1C Cantonment Road , part of The Pinnacle@Duxton , which was resold for $1.72 million — a fresh record at the development.

In Bishan, at the Natura Loft DBSS project, a unit changed hands for $1.6 million. The five-room flat sits on the 31st to 33rd storeys of Block 273A Bishan Street 24.

In the HDB leasing market, a four-room flat fetched the highest rent in the last 14 days, at $5,300 per month. Located at Block 17 Seng Poh Road in the Tiong Bahru neighbourhood, it is just opposite the Tiong Bahru Market hawker centre.

title: Sherman Kwek maps out CDL’s next three years: $5 bil to invest, $6 bil to divest
article:
Singapore-listed City Developments Ltd (CDL) intends to launch its high-rise condo in Shanghai’s Xintiandi in December. The luxury development will have 70 apartments, each measuring at least 400 sq m (4,306 sq ft).

A further 75 homes will be villas ranging from 250 sq m to 700 sq m, bringing the total to 145. The villas will be released in phases next year.

“These are going to be real trophy and iconic assets,” says CDL group CEO Sherman Kwek, at the company’s strategic review briefing on Sept 28.

CDL acquired the 27,994 sq m (about 301,325 sq ft) site in November 2024 for RMB8.94 billion ($1.66 billion at the time) through a 51:49 joint venture with Lianfa Group, whose controlling shareholder is the state-owned Xiamen C&D Group. CDL holds the 51% stake and is the lead developer.

In addition to luxury homes, the mixed-use development will include a boutique hotel and retail space. The site is in Shanghai’s Huangpu district, within walking distance of Xintiandi and Taipingqiao Park. Kwek calls it the “last remaining prime piece of land in Xintiandi”.

While China’s housing market is in its fifth year of decline, pockets of resilience remain in first-tier cities. Shanghai’s new home prices have risen for 12 of the past 13 months, the longest run among China’s first-tier cities, according to National Bureau of Statistics data cited by Nicholas Spiro in the South China Morning Post on Sept 14.

Demand for luxury homes remains strong in Shanghai’s prime districts, says Kwek, and Huangpu is “arguably one of the most desirable districts”.

On Sept 28, Shanghai issued implementation guidelines for national housing sale rules announced a month earlier. For residential sites whose land sale announcements were issued after Aug 28, developers are encouraged to sell completed homes. Those that choose to pre-sell must first complete the main structure of the building before launching units for sale.

That could push project launches to one to two years after a site is acquired, compared with about six to 10 months previously.

However, CDL is still targeting to launch its Xintiandi project before end of the year. “China’s real estate market is not in good shape. It’s under tremendous pressure, but there are still opportunities to be had,” says Kwek.

Sticking with GET

Xintiandi is one of several property bets under GET+, the refreshed three-year strategy unveiled at the briefing. It builds on the original GET strategy — Growth, Enhancement and Transformation — which Kwek introduced in 2018 after becoming CDL’s CEO.

Under GET+, CDL plans to make $5 billion of new investments and divest at least $6 billion of assets over FY2027 to FY2029. Of the new investment target, 60% will go to Singapore, 30% to China and Japan, and 10% to other markets. “It’s not good to be exposed and fully concentrated in one market, no matter how strong you are in that market,” says Kwek.

The investments will span four sectors: residential, commercial, hospitality and living, including rental housing such as the private rented sector (PRS), student accommodation and senior housing.

The market response was muted. CDL’s share price closed at $7.39 on Sept 30, down 10.5% from $8.26 before the strategic review was announced.

CDL, however, is taking a three-year view, and whether GET+ delivers will ultimately depend on execution. As Kwek said several times during the briefing: “The proof will be in the pudding.”

Kwek says CDL had considered replacing the GET strategy altogether, despite his having introduced it in 2018. Instead, after a year-long review, the group retained “its three pillars” while adding specific investment and divestment targets.

Under its GET strategy, CDL has sold more than 15,000 homes worth over $26 billion since 2018. It has also completed five major asset enhancement initiatives (AEIs), including those at Republic Plaza , where its headquarters is located, City Square Mall and Palais Renaissance in Singapore, and Jungceylon Shopping Center in Phuket, Thailand.

Banking on China

Kwek acknowledges that China’s inclusion in the investment plan is likely to raise eyebrows, describing it as “very much an opportunity bet”.

For the upcoming launch of the Xintiandi development, Kwek expects most buyers to be wealthy Shanghai residents. Buyers without Shanghai household registration must meet local residency, tax or social-security requirements, while foreign buyers are subject to separate eligibility rules.

He expects the 145 homes to generate “no less than RMB15 billion in sales value”, if all are sold.

“Currently, a lot of our hopes and expectations ride on our Xintiandi project in Shanghai,” he says.

He has taken his cue from nearby launches. In October 2024, Shui On Land launched the first phase of its Lakeville 6 residential project, facing Taipingqiao Lake in Xintiandi. All 108 units in the first phase, with a total gross floor area of 57,000 sq m, were taken up on launch day, generating RMB12 billion.

Land in Shanghai is costly. “One piece of land there can easily cost $2 billion and above,” says Kwek.

CDL was previously the sole developer of its projects in Chongqing and Suzhou. “Going forward, it will be more partnership-driven,” says Kwek. If Xintiandi performs well, CDL intends to pursue more projects with Lianfa Group.

Asked about the downside if the project underperformed, Kwek said: “If the project doesn’t sell well or tanks or something, then there’s not going to be a lot of confidence for management, especially for the board to approve future investments.”

In FY2020, CDL took a $1.78 billion impairment on its investment in Chongqing-based Sincere Property Group.

Exiting Australia’s non-hotel assets

CDL entered Australia in 2015 and has since undertaken several developments, including the Brickworks Park master-planned residential development in Brisbane, build-to-rent residential projects in Brisbane and Melbourne, and Zenith Residences in Sydney.

“It’s not a market that’s worked out too well for us, and we’ve been unable to build scale,” says Kwek.

CDL intends to divest its residential and commercial assets in Australia. That includes its 50% stake in the office tower at 330 Collins Street in Melbourne, which it co-invested alongside a fund in which CDL also has a stake.

“We have to ensure that it’s an orderly exit, so that we obtain the right exit price for the building,” says Kwek.

CDL will, however, keep its Australian hotels, such as Sofitel Brisbane Central, which it acquired in 2023, and the hotels in Brisbane and Perth held under CDL Hospitality Trusts.

Singapore: $3 bil for land and 2,200 homes in pipeline

About $3 billion (60%) of the new investment budget is earmarked for Singapore, which Kwek calls “business as usual”. The money will go into Government Land Sales (GLS), collective sales and off-market deals, though acquisitions will be “primarily GLS-driven”.

CDL’s current launch pipeline stands at 2,200 units after it won sites at Tanjong Rhu Road and Peck Hay Road this year.

The next test comes this weekend, on Oct 3, with the launch of the 570-unit Lucerne Grand at Lakeside Drive in Jurong West.

“If that substantially depletes our launch pipeline, then it’s time for us to replenish it,” says Kwek.

The rest of the pipeline comprises Tanjong Rhu Road, with about 515 units; Peck Hay Road, with about 380 units; and two executive condos, Solano Grand , with about 300 units, and Wynwood Grand , with about 430 units.

“In Singapore, no one can predict with a crystal ball how many land sales we can win in a year,” he says.

While CDL has raised its return targets for overseas investments, it has moderated its return expectations for Singapore land bids.

“If you’re going to have very high expectations and targets,” Kwek says of Singapore, “I may end up losing every single GLS tender.”

Redeveloping its own assets

CDL has another source of land: its own buildings. The 336-unit Union Square Residences is part of a mixed-use development that includes offices, retail and co-living components. It is a redevelopment of the former Central Mall and Central Square .

Newport Plaza, another mixed-use development with residences, offices, retail and serviced apartments, is targeted for completion next year. It is a redevelopment of the former Fuji Xerox Towers .

Two more assets are under study. CDL bought Delfi Orchard through a collective sale for $439 million in May 2024. The site sits next to its Orchard Hotel and Claymore Connect , and could be redeveloped together under the Strategic Development Incentive Scheme.

City House , which Kwek calls “our venerable iconic office building in the CBD”, could qualify for the CBD Incentive Scheme.

He has no intention of undertaking too many redevelopments at once. Redeveloping an existing building means giving up its rental income while taking on development loans.

“We don’t want too much happening at the same time. Otherwise it will put a lot of strain on us,” he says.

Rental housing as seed assets

CDL has also built up a living sector portfolio with a total gross development value of $3.7 billion, including pipeline projects.

It comprises 5,240 PRS units across Japan, Singapore, the UK and Australia, and 2,368 purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) beds in the UK.

The portfolio was built partly with fund management in mind. “It was also meant to form our seed assets for the fund management business, and that is still the case,” says Kwek.

Under GET+, CDL plans to sell suitable assets into funds and other vehicles it manages as it aims to double its assets under management from about $5 billion to $10 billion by FY2029.

When it does, Kwek prefers to hold no more than 20% of the fund, “so it will be a real divestment”.

Japan is the strongest performer, with 2,246 units.

“We have 40 operational PRS or multifamily assets in Japan, and they are doing really well for us, so there may be further expansion on that front,” he says.

In Singapore, recent additions include a standalone 35-storey serviced apartment tower at Zyon Grand under the SA2 long-stay serviced apartment category, which has a minimum stay of three months, and serviced apartments at Newport Plaza.

Not all the assets are ready to be sold into funds.

“Some of them, we may have to nurture for a bit longer, and stabilise over a period of time before we eventually turn it into a fund management vehicle,” says Kwek.

In the UK, CDL has 1,505 PRS units and 2,368 PBSA beds. The portfolio came under pressure when interest rates were high, and CDL is continuing to review it.

Hotel portfolio: Keep, fix or sell

The biggest review was of CDL’s hotel portfolio. Of the group’s 88 owned hotels, 54 are directly held by CDL and valued at about $8.6 billion.

“We went through every single hotel,” says Kwek.

The directly held portfolio has been split into three groups. About $5 billion worth of hotels will be retained, around $1.8 billion will be enhanced through renovation or redevelopment, and another $1.8 billion will be divested.

The exercise reflects GET+’s broader push to distinguish between assets CDL intends to hold and enhance, and those where capital can be recycled.

Freeing up trapped capital

Kwek says the group has identified more than $6 billion of potential divestments, giving it scope to exceed its $6 billion target.

But he will not sell at any price. This year, he says, CDL had several potential sales in hand but chose not to proceed. “I would be leaving money on the table,” he says.

Of the $6 billion divestment target, commercial assets make up 45% and hotels 30%. Legacy residential assets, including an $800 million UK portfolio, account for 20%, while living assets make up 5%.

According to Kwek, legacy residential assets include some in Singapore, such as the 59 units CDL still holds at the 110-unit freehold Cliveden at Grange, completed in 2011.

“Even in Singapore, we have some legacy residential that we need to get going when it comes to recycling the capital that’s been trapped there for quite a while,” he says.

In December 2023, CDL sold the loss-making Millennium Harvest House in Boulder, Colorado, for $94.4 million and recognised an $80 million gain. According to Kwek, the buyer intended to convert the property into student housing.

What keeps him going

At the end of the two-hour briefing, an analyst asked Kwek what still motivates him to lead CDL despite the scrutiny that comes with the job.

Kwek pointed to his grandfather, Hong Leong Group founder Kwek Hong Png.

“I think I’ve always been driven by the fact that I want to perpetuate the legacy, our family legacy,” he says. “My grandfather had a very deep and meaningful influence on me when I was growing up.”

When Republic Plaza was refurbished, Kwek turned part of the ground floor into a founder’s gallery depicting his grandfather’s life and how he built up Hong Leong Group and CDL.

In 2018, when he was 42 and a new CEO,  Kwek said: “We cannot rest on our laurels. A lot needs to be done, especially in this day and age of disruption and innovation.”

He now adds: “I used to think that career was everything in life, and the be-all and end-all. But after you start having a family and kids, you realise that there are other aspects of life as well.”

He admits he is “still unable to strike a work-life balance”. But his sense of responsibility to the family legacy remains — and with it, his commitment to CDL.

title: Why Far East Organization waited 16 years to launch freehold The Serra Residences in Novena
article:
When Far East Organization bought the Pastoral View apartment complex en bloc in 2010, HealthCity Novena was little more than a plan.

Sixteen years on, with the medical hub taking shape around it, the developer is turning the site into The Serra Residences , a 133-unit freehold condo that opens for preview on Oct 2. The official launch is slated for Oct 16.

The site at 7 Bassein Road sits in prime District 11, bounded by Bassein Road, Akyab Road and Tan Tock Seng Link.

Search for the latest New Launches , to find out the transaction prices and available units

Far East Organization and its joint-venture partner Far East Orchard (then Orchard Parade Holdings) paid a combined $122 million for Pastoral View and the adjacent vacant plot at 11 Bassein Road, which was owned by OCBC Bank.

The combined site area is 51,396 sq ft, and the price works out to about $848 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr), inclusive of development charges.

A 16-year hold

Although Pastoral View was built in 1986, it was well-maintained when Far East Organization and Far East Orchard acquired it. Instead of redeveloping the site, the joint-venture partners refurbished its 50 apartments, added some furnishing and leased them out.

The units comprised one-bedroom units of 614 sq ft, two-bedroom units of 990 sq ft, and three-bedroom units of 1,259 to 1,500 sq ft.

“The occupancy was always around 95%,” says Shaw Lay See, COO of Far East Organization. Tenants were mainly expatriates, from medical professionals in Novena to those working in the CBD, Orchard Road and the city fringe. They ranged from singles to couples and families, drawn by the amenities in the area.

In 2015, Far East Orchard sold its stake to its parent, Far East Organization, giving the latter full control of the two adjoining sites. The combined site has a plot ratio of 2.8 and a maximum height of 36 storeys. Even so, Far East Organization held off on redevelopment and continued to lease out the units.

HealthCity Novena was conceived in 2009 by the Ministry of Health, Tan Tock Seng Hospital (TTSH) and the National Healthcare Group . But the master plan for the 17ha medical campus, about the size of 24 football pitches, was officially launched only in 2013.

According to Shaw, the area was still evolving in 2010, and Far East Organization felt it was too early to launch a new project. “It was hard for people to visualise what it would look like in the future,” she says of that time.

An early mover in Novena

Far East Organization has been in Novena since 2002, when it won the Government Land Sale (GLS) tender for the Novena Medical Centre site.

Novena Medical Centre was completed in 2006, followed in 2007 by Square 2 mall, which links Novena Medical Centre to Novena MRT Station.

In 2007, Far East Organization also won the GLS tender for a 99-year leasehold hotel and commercial site at 8 Sinaran Drive. It has since been developed into the 428-room Oasia Hotel Novena and the adjacent Novena Specialist Centre, both linked underground to Square 2 and Novena MRT Station. The development was completed in 2011.

Far East Organization has also developed two freehold condos in Novena. They are the 100-unit Strata on Essex Road, launched in 2003 and completed in 2006; and the 85-unit Miro on Lincoln Road, launched in 2008 and completed in 2012.

“For the past 20 years, we have developed more than seven projects cutting across the residential, medical, retail and hospitality sectors,” says Shaw. “So we are very familiar with this location, and we believe in the fundamentals of this location.”

A neighbourhood transformed

The first phase of HealthCity Novena was completed in 2024. It includes the National Centre for Infectious Diseases, the TTSH Integrated Care Hub, which helps patients move from acute care to rehabilitation before returning home, and the Ng Teng Fong Centre for Healthcare Innovation.

The Lee Kong Chian School of Medicine Novena campus, developed jointly by Nanyang Technological University and Imperial College London, was completed in 2017. A new National Skin Centre opened in 2023, doubling capacity and cutting median waiting times by 30%.

The second phase of HealthCity Novena master plan, launched in September 2025, will run beyond 2030. It includes a new TTSH Medical Tower, which will add about 600 acute beds and expand the emergency department.

“As Singapore’s population ages, healthcare will become an increasingly important pillar of the economy, making the continued expansion of Health-City Novena a significant long-term driver for the precinct,” says Marcus Chu, CEO of ERA Singapore.

Last December, the Singapore Land Authority awarded the tender for the 985,350 sq ft site at 2 Moulmein Road to Country City Investment, which has developed and managed the Dempsey Hill lifestyle and dining enclave since 2007.

The site has 44 conservation buildings and has been approved for co-living, wellness, health and fitness, pet-friendly services, an art gallery and educational programmes. About 41,900 sq ft of its gross floor area of 139,700 sq ft can be used for F&B and retail. It is targeted to open in 1Q2027.

Shaw expects the new lifestyle hub to make the neighbourhood more vibrant. What’s more, The Serra is located within walking distance from it.

Construction is also underway on the 21.5km North-South Corridor, which will link northern Singapore to the city centre and ease congestion on the Central Expressway. The northern viaduct sections will open in phases from 2029, and the tunnel sections from 2031.

Why now?

With these projects in progress, Far East Organization began rethinking its plans for Pastoral View and the adjacent plot. Pastoral View also turns 40 this year, and keeping it would mean spending more on maintenance as wear and tear sets in.

That was when Far East Organization’s management began to question holding on to the building.

“So we asked ourselves: Do we really want to continue putting money into an old building, when the market is telling us that the location is ready for redevelopment?” says Shaw.

Core Central Region (CCR) launches this year have seen healthy take-up over their launch weekends, including Newport Residences (57%) in January, River Modern (90%) in March, and Dunearn House (56%) in July. Of the four CCR projects launched so far this year, only Newport Residences is freehold.

Buoyed by that demand, Far East Organization is launching The Serra, the second freehold launch in the CCR this year.

Inspired by Zhangjiajie’s quartz-sandstone pillars

Designed by P&T Consultants, the 28-storey tower covers about 30% of the site. Homes start on Level 4, about 25m above street level, which is equivalent to about eight storeys in a typical condo.

The units are split into two zones. The Serra Residences, on levels 4 to 16, have 91 units: two-bedroom-plus-study, three-bedroom and four-bedroom units of 710 to 958 sq ft.

The Summit , on levels 18 to 28, has 42 units. They comprise 20 four-bedroom and four-bedroom-plus-study units of 1,216 to 1,335 sq ft, and 20 four- and five-bedroom premium units of 1,528 to 1,755 sq ft.

Two five-bedroom penthouses of 2,648 sq ft and 2,669 sq ft crown the tower. The premium units and penthouses, 22 in all, come with private lifts.

The tower has a north-south orientation, maximising cross-ventilation and cutting the western sun, while travertine fins on its east and west façades provide further shade.

Its design draws on the quartz-sandstone pillars of Zhangjiajie National Forest Park in China’s Hunan province, which are said to have inspired James Cameron’s movie Avatar.

According to Kingsley Ng, architect and director at P&T Consultants, the tower is carved into layered voids to create elevated green terraces for residents.

Shaw says The Serra has a wellness theme. With just 133 units, it includes a full-sized tennis court, a 50m lap pool, a gym, function rooms, a children’s playground, and even a pet park. The sky terrace on Level 17 has a wellness garden, a lounge and a quiet zone for yoga, as well as senior-friendly fitness equipment.

The car park has 113 parking lots, including two dedicated spots for the penthouses and five EV charging spots. It also has 23 bicycle parking spaces.

The Serra is expected to obtain its temporary occupation permit in 4Q2030.

The first new launch in five years

According to Huttons Asia, the last new launch in the Novena neighbourhood of District 11 was five years ago: the 90-unit freehold Peak Residence on Thomson Road. Developed by Tuan Sing Holdings and Rich Capital Holdings, it was launched in April 2021 and completed in 2025.

Before that came the 87-unit freehold Neu at Novena on Moulmein Rise, developed by a consortium of Roxy-Pacific Holdings, Macly Group and LWH Holdings. It was launched in October 2019 and completed in 2023.

On Oct 2, Far East Organization announced that prices will start from $3,120 psf for a 710 sqft, two-bedroom with study unit which translates to $2.22 million.

The latest transaction at Neu at Novena was for an 818 sq ft, three-bedroom dual-key unit that changed hands for $2.39 million ($2,922 psf), according to a caveat lodged in August 2026.

Prices of new launches are likely to climb further. According to PropNex Research, recent CCR GLS sites have been awarded at $1,865 psf ppr for Peck Hay Road and $1,820 psf ppr for Bukit Timah Road. Based on these land prices, PropNex estimates that future CCR projects could cross $3,500 psf.

Kelvin Fong, CEO of PropNex, notes that several recent CCR launches have achieved average prices above $3,000 psf. “The market has demonstrated that buyers are willing to transact at these levels for well-located prime projects. Meanwhile, rising land costs are likely to place further upward pressure on future private home prices of 99-year leasehold projects in the CCR.”

PropNex Research also shows that the premium for new freehold launches has narrowed sharply. The median price of new freehold launches in the CCR was about $3,160 psf in 3Q2026, against about $3,110 psf for 99-year leasehold launches. That is a gap of roughly 1.6%, down from more than 37% in 2018.

Freehold for the long haul

Yet freehold land is increasingly scarce. Of the close to 4,000 new private non-landed homes launched in the CCR from 1Q2024 to 2Q2026, only 287, or 7%, were freehold, according to Huttons Asia.

“When considering two new launches in the same location, the premium between freehold and leasehold may not mean much. But 20 years down the road, when you want to resell, there will be a difference,” says Shaw. “That’s because the value of the property is the land, and not the building.”

Huttons’ data bears this out. Since 2015, resale freehold non-landed homes in the CCR have appreciated 36%, against 25% for 99-year leasehold non-landed homes.

Affluent buyers recognise the long-term value of freehold tenure, says Shaw. Far East Organization’s freehold Amber House, launched in June 2025, is 83% sold at an average of $3,055 psf, based on caveats lodged as at Sept 29.

The 105-unit Amber House is a redevelopment of the former Amber Glades, which Far East Organization acquired en bloc for $118.1 million in March 2011. As with The Serra, it held on to the site for a long time — 14 years — before launching.

Many of the buyers were older purchasers acquiring homes for their children, says Shaw. They preferred the four-bedroom units starting from $5 million. “They are buying for future generations.”

“The Serra Residences is one of the only two freehold launches in the CCR in 2026,” says Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia. “It offers buyers an opportunity to own a freehold non-landed home in the CCR for both wealth preservation and legacy planning.”

Rental demand

Given The Serra’s proximity to HealthCity Novena, SRI managing partner Ken Low expects buyers to be a mix of owner-occupiers and investors.

According to SRI’s research based on URA data, more than 1,000 private residential rental contracts were signed in the Novena Planning Area every quarter from 1Q2025 to 2Q2026. Volume rose 13.5% q-o-q to 1,262 contracts in 2Q2026.

Rents have held up as well. Two-bedroom units in Novena averaged $4,506 a month in 2Q2026, the highest since 1Q2025, according to SRI. “Demand spans a range of tenants, from healthcare professionals to families drawn to nearby schools, while larger four-bedroom homes continue to command significantly higher rents,” says Low.

St Joseph’s Institution Junior and Hong Wen School are within 1km of The Serra, and Novena MRT Station is an eight-minute walk away. Nearby malls include Square 2, Velocity and United Square.

No pressure to sell

Far East Organization acquired Pastoral View in 2010, before the additional buyer’s stamp duty (ABSD) was extended to developers in December 2011. The site is therefore not subject to the five-year ABSD remission deadline, which requires developers to complete a project and sell all its residential units within five years. That five-year deadline applies to more recent collective-sale and GLS sites.

“For The Serra Residences, we’re not under a deadline to sell, so we can take a measured approach to pricing,” says Shaw. “Our prices will reflect today’s market and the quality of what we’re delivering. We’re focused on the project’s long-term value, rather than on reducing prices to move units quickly. With just 133 homes, the choice of units will naturally be limited.”

title: 3 Singapore Stocks That Have Raised Their Dividends consistently over the past 5 Years
article:
Companies that consistently raise their dividends are demonstrating something real: growing earnings, cash generation, and more importantly, a willingness to share more of it with shareholders.
But a growth streak proves nothing about the future.
Three companies stand out for raising their dividends steadily over the past five years.
The real question is whether they can do it again over
the next five
.
What Makes a Dividend-Growth Stock Attractive?
A few things separate a genuine dividend grower from a company that just happens to pay more this year.
Earnings need to be rising, giving the business room to pay out more without straining itself.
The earnings growth should also show up in cash, not just on paper — a company can report a healthy profit and still struggle to pay a dividend if the cash isn’t there.
The payout ratio matters too: pay out too little, and shareholders miss out; pay out too much, and there’s nothing left to reinvest.
And debt should stay manageable, since a business weighed down by loans has far less room to keep paying a dividend when conditions turn tough.
A bonus point if the business has a special sauce, such as a regulatory moat, that helps keep growth humming through different business cycles.
DBS (SGX: D05) – The Blue-Chip Dividend Grower
This financial powerhouse has seen its dividend nearly triple since 2021 – from S$1.09 per share to S$3.06 in 2025, which represents a 29% compound annual growth rate (CAGR).
Moreover, the dividend has been on a mostly consistent upward path, with only 2023’s dividend dipping compared to the prior year.
It’s not hard to see why DBS’s dividend growth has been so robust. In the latest quarter ending 30 June 2026 (Q2 2026), DBS posted record total income and net profit of S$6.1 billion and S$3.1 billion, respectively. The former grew 6% year-on-year (YoY) while the latter was up 9% and supported a strong return on equity (ROE) of 17.9%.
There is room for further dividend increases given DBS’s payout ratio for ordinary dividends is only around 30%, while a healthy fully phased-in common equity tier one (CET1) ratio of 14.6% provides decent support for continued payments through tough times.
Finally, a booming wealth management business further supports the possibility of dividend growth being continued moving forward.
Singapore Exchange (SGX: 68), or SGX – The Defensive Dividend Compounder
SGX’s total dividend rose from S$0.32 per share in FY2021 (financial year ended 30 June 2021) to S$0.57 per share in FY2026 – a 12.2% CAGR over five years, although the dividend-record includes one flat year in FY2022.
As a toll-booth business that effectively levies a tax on trading activity in Singapore’s financial market, SGX’s earnings and free cash flow (FCF) hold up even during weaker economic periods; this is best seen in its historical dividend payments, which have held even during weaker markets.
Further dividend growth comes down to SGX’s ability to maintain its steady revenue growth over the years and a historically disciplined payout ratio (around 60-80% of earnings). The bourse operator’s solid balance sheet with minimal net debt further fortifies its future dividend payments.
ST Engineering (SGX: S63) – The Higher-Growth Dividend Payer
The last name on this list may not have consistently increased its dividends year after year, but its five-year track record is nothing to scoff at: ST Engineering’s total dividend rose from S$0.15 per share in 2021 to S$0.23 in 2025 – an 11.3% CAGR.
Although the starting and current yields are low, ST Engineering’s dividend growth has outpaced inflation on the back of a robust order book (S$35.7 billion as of 30 June 2026), strong free cash flow generation, and healthy secular growth trends in ST Engineering’s key markets of aerospace and defence.
As long as the company keeps winning orders and does a solid job of converting its order book into earnings and cash flow, it is likely that ST Engineering continues raising its dividends.
This is especially so given management’s new dividend policy to pay out more of its earnings to shareholders.
Why Dividend Growth Can Matter More Than a High Starting Yield
A simple illustration: Stock A yields 6% today but never raises its payout, while Stock B starts at 3.5% but grows its dividend 7% a year.
On a S$10,000 stake, Stock A pays S$600 a year, indefinitely. Stock B starts at S$350 — but compounding at 7%, it overtakes Stock A’s income within about eight years, and keeps pulling further ahead every year after.
This is yield on cost: your income measured against your original
investment, not today’s price. A dividend that keeps growing can turn a modest starting yield into a substantial one over a long enough horizon — the inverse of what a static high yield can ever do.
What Could Break the Dividend Growth Streak?
Watch for
earnings declines
, weakening free cash flow, a payout ratio stretching beyond what earnings can support, sharply rising debt, heavy new capex requirements, industry disruption, or management choosing to prioritise acquisitions over the dividend.
Past growth is useful evidence, but you still have to monitor if cash generation supports dividend payments.
What Should Investors Watch Going Forward?
As always, monitor quarterly earnings and whether they translate into free cash flow. We also do not want a material increase in debt from companies to fund their payments.
The best dividend growers are simply businesses whose earnings and cash flow keep growing alongside what they pay out — not the other way around.
Get Smart: Look for Dividends That Can Keep Growing
DBS, SGX and ST Engineering have all
raised their dividends
over the past five years, but not one of them did it every single year — each had a flat or uneven stretch somewhere along the way.
That’s worth remembering before crediting any company with a clean streak.
The dividend itself is really just the output.
What decides whether it keeps rising is the business behind it: are earnings actually growing, is that growth turning into real cash, does the balance sheet have room to absorb a bad year?
Check those, and the yield on the label matters a lot less.
Over a long horizon, a steadily rising dividend — even an imperfect one — can become a genuinely powerful source of compounding income.
Retirement doesn’t happen overnight. It’s built one decision at a time.

title: Top SGX Stocks Q3 2026: Only 4 Blue Chips Beat the STI
article:
It was a good quarter to own
Singapore blue chips
.
The
SPDR STI ETF
(SGX: ES3), which tracks the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI), delivered a total return of 11.6% in 3Q2026.
Four stocks did better.
Yangzijiang Shipbuilding (Holdings) Ltd.
(SGX: BS6), or YZJ, led the pack with a 50.3% return.
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, followed with 31%,
DBS Group Holdings
(SGX: D05) hit 20.2% and
Hongkong Land Holdings Limited
(SGX: H78) generated 13.7%.
All four figures are total returns, which means they include
dividends
.
Their latest results give us a few clues about what caught investors’ eyes.
Can YZJ keep its shipyards full?
YZJ’s revenue rose 36% year on year (YoY) to RMB17.5 billion in the first half of 2026 (1H2026).
Its shipbuilding gross margin widened to 37% from 35%, while profit attributable to shareholders climbed 28% to RMB5.4 billion.
The driver here is execution on higher-value contracts.
YZJ is now building ships it won at better prices, such as ultra-large containerships and very large ethane carriers.
Its new Hongyuan yard also began contributing, chipping in RMB545 million of revenue in the second quarter.
Is the cash keeping pace with the profit? Not quite yet.
Free cash flow rose 82% to RMB675.4 million, which is only an eighth of attributable profit.
Since free cash flow ultimately funds dividends, this gap is worth keeping an eye on.
That said, YZJ has plenty of runway.
It held RMB15.9 billion in cash against RMB4.1 billion of borrowings as at 30 June 2026.
The group pays dividends annually, with its FY2025 final dividend of S$0.20 per share paid out in May 2026.
YZJ’s order book stood at US$22.4 billion.
By July 2026, it had secured about US$1.96 billion in new orders, putting it 43.6% of the way towards its FY2026 target of US$4.5 billion.
How did OCBC post a record half on thinner margins?
OCBC earned less on each dollar it lent, as its net interest margin (NIM) narrowed to 1.73% in 1H2026 from 1.98% a year ago.
That pushed net interest income down 3% YoY to S$4.5 billion, though 12% loan growth helped cushion the impact.
The bank made up the shortfall through non-interest income, which surged 36% to S$3.5 billion.
A pickup in wealth management activity boosted fees and commissions by 26%, while trading income climbed 46% and insurance income rose 49%.
Together, these drivers pushed net profit up 13% to a record S$4.2 billion.
The board raised the interim dividend 14.6% to S$0.47 per share, maintaining a 50% payout ratio.
On 7 August 2026, management upgraded its FY2026 guidance and now expects net interest income to decline only slightly.
What pushed DBS past S$6 billion in quarterly income?
Reporting on a quarterly schedule, DBS delivered total income of S$6.1 billion for 2Q2026, up 6% YoY.
It marks the first time the bank has crossed the S$6 billion threshold in a single quarter.
DBS felt the same margin pressure as OCBC.
Its NIM narrowed to 1.87% from 2.05%, causing net interest income to slip 2% to S$3.6 billion.
Wealth management stepped up here as well.
Wealth fees jumped 42% to S$919 million, pushing net fee and commission income up 25% to S$1.5 billion.
Net profit rose 9% to S$3.1 billion, yielding a return on equity (ROE) of 17.9%.
DBS declared two payouts for the quarter:
Ordinary interim dividend: S$0.66 per share
Capital return dividend: S$0.15 per share
Like OCBC, DBS raised its full-year guidance and now expects total income for 2026 to top its 2025 performance.
How does Hongkong Land earn more when operating profit stays flat?
Hongkong Land
‘s operating profit barely moved in 1H2026, coming in at US$318.9 million.
Underlying profit still rose 11% YoY to US$259.1 million.
The group recycled capital through asset sales, helping cut net financing charges by 36% to US$56.2 million.
A lower share count provided an extra boost, driving underlying earnings per share (EPS) up 14% to US$0.1207.
Shareholders received a higher payout as the interim dividend rose 33% to US$0.08 per share, representing about 66% of underlying EPS.
Free cash flow went in the opposite direction, dropping 26% to US$153.2 million as renovation spending nearly doubled.
Net gearing remained manageable at 11%.
Investors should look past the headline profit figure of US$1.3 billion.
More than half of that stems from a US$725.1 million revaluation gain, which is a paper adjustment rather than an actual cash inflow.
What do the four outperformers share?
At OCBC, DBS and Hongkong Land, the main earnings engine stalled, but profits grew anyway.
The
banks
leaned on wealth management fees as their margins shrank, while Hongkong Land trimmed its interest bill.
YZJ is the odd one out, simply earning better margins across its shipyards.
All four gave the market clear reason for confidence.
OCBC, DBS and Hongkong Land raised their dividends or upgraded guidance, while YZJ reaffirmed its order target.
Get Smart: Find the engine
A strong quarter tells you a stock has run, but it cannot tell you whether the run will last.
To answer that, look at which engine produced the profit, and assess whether it can keep running.
For OCBC and DBS, watch whether wealth fees keep growing when markets turn quiet.
Hongkong Land has already completed 93% of its capital recycling target, meaning room for further interest savings is limited.
YZJ still needs another US$2.54 billion in contract wins to hit its FY2026 goal.

title: A Tipping Point for the Stock Market
article:
THE US Treasury might like to talk tough. Secretary Scott Bessent’s latest salvo was directed at foreign-exchange traders. He warned them against betting against the US dollar.
“I am the house now… you can bet against me if you want,” he told them. He was referring specifically to the US Treasury’s support for the yen.
Bessent might just be able to pull off his audacious support for the Japanese currency, but only if the Bank of Japan plays ball by raising interest rates.
Fooling around with currencies is one thing, but playing fast and loose with the bond market, especially with US Treasuries, is another.
He actually believes that he can suppress long-term interest rates by buying back US$6 billion worth of 30-year Treasuries. By pushing up the bonds’ prices, he hopes to force down the yield on them.
Worryingly, Bessent is missing the point about why the market is selling Treasuries. It has nothing to do with betting against the “house”.
Pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, insurance companies and family offices are not gamblers. They are selling Treasuries because they believe that the Federal Reserve is not doing its job properly. They also think that America is being reckless with its finances.
Who holds the cards?
Bond investors were always going to decide where US interest rates should be. They weigh up many factors before they decide whether to lend money to the US government.
The Trump administration might think that it can influence and cajole the Fed. But the reality is that the Fed, and even the US Treasury, is powerless against bondholders.
It would be different if America does not have to borrow money – but it does.
Its national debt is US$40 trillion dollars and rising. Annual payments on these loans exceed US$1 trillion and are going up, too. That is why bond investors are worried.
To borrow a phrase from US President Donald Trump, America does not have the cards. Lenders will always have the upper hand.
Meanwhile, the Treasury secretary might also like to think that he can manipulate interest rates by selling short-duration debt and buying 30-year Treasuries.
But bondholders will not be fooled that easily. For every dollar of long-dated Treasuries that Scott Bessent should buy, bondholders can sell much more.
Pragmatism reigns
Bondholders are essentially pragmatic investors. They just want the Fed to do the right thing, which is to tame inflation. There is only one tool that it has in its armoury to do that effectively, which is to raise
interest rates
.
It is quite unacceptable that the US inflation rate has been allowed to stay above the Fed’s target for more than five years. And of those five years, two have been under a Trump administration.
Currently, there are few signs that the inflation rate will return to 2 per cent, given that global supply chains have been fractured by Trump.
The Iran war, which was started by the president, has exacerbated inflationary pressures by pushing up energy prices. Brent crude is trading
above US$100
a barrel. If we throw in climate change, which Trump claims is a hoax, then we could see persistently higher food prices too.
The outlook for inflation does not look good if things should stay as they are. It could worsen unless central banks act decisively.
This is not just a US problem. Many economies also face similar issues. Furthermore, many countries are probably reaching the limit that they can comfortably borrow.
Shock and awe
It will not be pleasant for stock market investors if bondholders continue to flex their muscles. We are closing in on a tipping point for shares. The 10-year Treasury yield is fast approaching 5 per cent.
Meanwhile, the US market is valued at 25 times earnings, which implies an earnings yield of 4 per cent. Even Singapore’s Straits Times Index (SGX: ^STI) is valued at 20 times earnings, which suggests an earnings yield of 5 per cent.
When investors have a choice between a risk-free asset that offers a yield close to 5 per cent and a risk asset with a more unpredictable future, then they could have a reason to think twice. Whether the Fed raises interest rates becomes a moot point.
But this could be just the time for investors to look at businesses with dependable cash flow, high returns on equity and a strong track record of rewarding investors with regular dividends.
As an income investor, any correction in share prices that might ensue could be an
opportunity
to buy more rising income from good companies.
Investing is never about trying to second-guess where share prices might be tomorrow or what the Fed might do at its next meeting. It is about working out the yield on an asset over its lifetime.
In other words, it is about buying wonderful companies at fair prices and holding them for the long term.
